entries.title: Customer support is the gnarliest AI problem
entries.summary: Ryan chats with Ahmad Al-Dahle, CTO at Airbnb, about deploying multi-party AI agents to tackle the uniquely gnarly problem of customer support, how a moving target of rigorous evaluations helps engineers balance latency against accuracy, and the ways in which AI coding tools demand an even higher level of judgment from software engineering teams.
entries.content:
Ryan chats with Ahmad Al-Dahle, CTO at Airbnb, about deploying multi-party AI agents to tackle the uniquely gnarly problem of customer support, how a moving target of rigorous evaluations helps engineers balance latency against accuracy, and the ways in which AI coding tools demand an even higher level of judgment from software engineering teams.

Learn more about how Airbnb is evolving its engineering organization to implement generative AI across the platform on their tech blog.

entries.title: Never Share Your Password Again — The OAuth 2.0 Solution
entries.content:
Before OAuth 2.0 existed, if you wanted a third-party app to read your Twitter timeline, you had to give them your Twitter username and password. Not a token, not a scoped credential your actual password.

The app would log in as you, do what it needed, and (if you were lucky) not store the password anywhere sketchy. Users did this constantly. Whole categories of app worked this way Twitter clients, mail readers, contact importers, calendar syncers. Every one of them held a growing collection of user passwords.

This was called the password anti-pattern and it was as bad as it sounds. If the third party app got breached, every user account it touched went with it. Users could not revoke access to a single app without changng their password everywhere. The app had full account access, not just the piece it actually needed.

What OAuth 2.0 does - The user authenticates only with the service they trust (Google, GitHub, etc.). The third-party app never sees the password. The service issues the app a token, and the token carries three important properties:

1. Scoped — It grants only the specific permissions the user approved. 2. Time-limited — It expires, usually within an hour.

3. Revocable — The user can kill it any time from their account settings. The actual flow

The modern standard is Authorization Code with PKCE. Five steps. 1. The app redirects the user to the authorization server.

https://auth.example.com/oauth/authorize

?response_type=code

&client_id=budgettrack-prod

&redirect_uri=https://budgettrack.com/callback

&scope=calendar.read

&state=xY7f3aQ2

&code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM &code_challenge_method=S256

2. The user authenticates on the auth server's own domain.

The third-party app never sees this happen. No password crosses the network to anyone but the auth server itself.

3. The auth server redirects back with a short-lived code.

https://budgettrack.com/callback

?code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA

&state=xY7f3aQ2

4. The app exchanges the code for a token, server-to-server.

POST /oauth/token HTTP/1.1

Host: auth.example.com

Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code

&code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA

&redirect_uri=https://budgettrack.com/callback

&client_id=budgettrack-prod

&code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk

5. The auth server returns the token.

json

{

"access_token": "eyJhbGci...",

"token_type": "Bearer",

"expires_in": 3600,

"refresh_token": "v1.MRn7...",

"scope": "calendar.read"

}

The app now calls the API with Authorization: Bearer until the token expires. The user's password was never involved at any point.

What those magic parameters actually do?

The flow above has four security-critical parameters that most tutorials gloss over. Here is what each one is defending against.

state=xY7f3aQ2 CSRF protection. The app generates a random value, sends it in the authorize request, and checks that the same value comes back on the redirect. Without

this, an attacker could trick a signed-in user into completing the attacker's OAuth flow, binding the attacker's account to the user's app session. Not checking state is one of the most common OAuth bugs in the wild.

code_challenge + code_verifier PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange). The app generates a random code_verifier, hashes it with SHA-256 to produce the code_challenge sent in step 1, then presents the original code_verifier when exchanging the code in step 4. This defeats any attacker who intercepts the authorization code without the matching code_verifier, the stolen code is worthless. Required for mobile apps and SPAs; strongly recommended everywhere else.

redirect_uri=https://budgettrack.com/callback The auth server will only send the code to this exact URL, pre-registered with the auth server. Attackers cannot swap in https://evil.com/callback to hijack the code mid-flight.

Short-lived code (step 3) The authorization code is single-use and expires in seconds (typically 10 seconds to 2 minutes). Even if captured in a log or network trace, it cannot be reused later.

Four small parameters. Each one closes a specific attack. Together they are the reason OAuth 2.0 is secure enough to run every "Sign in with Google" button on the internet.

Why scopes matter - scope=calendar.read means the app can read the calendar. That is it. It cannot delete events, cannot send email, cannot access contacts, cannot post on the user's behalf. If the app gets breached tomorrow, the attacker has read access to calendars. Bad, but bounded.

Compare this to the pre-OAuth world where the attacker would have had full account access to every service the app touched, everywhere. The whole game of security is turning "everything" into "one specific thing," and scopes are how OAuth 2.0 does it at the protocol level.

Summary - OAuth 2.0 exists so a user can grant a third-party app scoped, time limited, revocable access to their account without ever handing over their password. Everything else in the protocol code exchanges, refresh tokens, PKCE, scopes, discovery is machinery in service of that one principle.

entries.title: Welcome to life in the chip age
entries.summary: Ryan sits down with Rakesh Kumar, professor of computer engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, about the astounding complexity of manufacturing modern semiconductors, the massive environmental and geopolitical footprint of AI data centers, and how AI models are rapidly shifting the future of chip design.
entries.content:
Ryan sits down with Rakesh Kumar, professor of computer engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, about the astounding complexity of manufacturing modern semiconductors, the massive environmental and geopolitical footprint of AI data centers, and how AI models are rapidly shifting the future of chip design.

Dive deeper into the history and future of semiconductors by checking out Rakesh's book, The Chip Age.

entries.title: Don’t Build the Reusable Component Yet
entries.content:
Everyone who ever worked in frontend knows what kind of advice they are going to receive: to make things reusable. Find similar screens, create an abstracted component. Now, enjoy the little pleasure of deleting extra code. However, sometimes there are cases when I would like to say the exact opposite of this, for a short period of time, at least. Not only does the creation of an abstracted component mean higher costs of coding but also higher costs of coordination.

Duplication can easily be removed, but a wrong abstraction can be expensive to undo.

The case: one component, three workflows

In old days, there were three workflows, where I had to perform an “item action,” which consisted of workflow approval ("Do you really need this item?"), workflow change ("Change item's settings"), and workflow movement ("Move item from/to managed area").

There was nothing unusual about the interface for these actions – item list, select, confirm, and show the results. Same tables, pop-ups, and toasts. It just seemed ridiculous to create three almost identical actions; so, I decided to create only one.

What I did not understand back then is that the similarities were only on the surface. I have not understood how each of those processes deals with partial failure, what are the requirements for each of them, and what information should be gathered for auditing purposes. Approval of an item action is an assertion about the future ("I will need this item"). Modification occurs instantly. Relocation requires another system to accept the request, and that system may reject it.

How it went wrong: flags, modes and a growing list of exceptions

The first iteration only featured one object that was important. After several weeks, it became more or less like this (an illustration, not the actual code):

      
type Item = { id: string; name: string };

    
      
type ItemActionProps = {
  item: Item;
  mode: "approve" | "change" | "move";
  variant?: "inline" | "dialog" | "bulk";
  showDetails?: boolean;
  requireReason?: boolean;
  onSpecialCase?: (item: Item) => boolean;
};

    
      
function ItemAction({ item, mode, variant, showDetails, requireReason, onSpecialCase }: ItemActionProps) {
  if (mode === "move" && onSpecialCase?.(item)) {
    return ;   // only moves need this
  }
  const needsReason = mode === "change" || requireReason;
  // ...three submit paths, three error shapes, one component
}

All those were justified additions. The formula was that each additional screen came with a justification why this particular component could not be changed. Each additional requirement on the moves required a new flag. If that flag was cumbersome, the other alternative was a change of shared behavior, and then it had to be verified that approvals and changes still work.

Any change to the confirmation procedure could no longer be done by the owner of the workflow, but would require agreement from all three owners, the reviewer who knew all the modes, and test cases for all the combinations of mode and variant. An alteration in one area led to an argument about all the others.

Why it happens

Indeed, there are multiple advantages for applying the earlier mentioned approach to abstraction. Cleaner code is good code. The diff that allows eliminating two hundred lines of code deserves to be appreciated. The consistency seems to be another rational way of approaching the design.

In this case, all you have is the information in the current state. Many other similar cases show you that many cases have some common attributes. However, they cannot tell you about the differences between them, because the differences will be evident in the future: new policy, new audit finding, new integration that does not behave as you expected.

This means that the abstraction is based on current similarities, while any differences will have no other thing to do but to serve as flags.

The rule: wait for three, then check the reasons

However, until the pattern is repeated three times with the same reason for changing, wait. In the meantime, simply grab the code and let each screen evolve on its own.

This second half is equally important as the first half. Two codes share the same reason for change when a single decision made by a single individual changes both at the same time. Take a look at these:

      
// Same reason to change: one product decision about how dates look.
formatExpiry(item.expiresAt)   // approve, change and move screens

    
      
// Different reasons, despite identical-looking code:
await api.post("/approve", body); toast.success("Done");   // changes with approval policy
await api.post("/change", body);  toast.success("Done");   // changes with validation rules

Date formatter is fine to extract since changing formats affects all screens. Submit buttons appear duplicated but belong to different owners. Combining them binds two unrelated decisions together.

My test is, "In the case of change to this requirement, who would I consult, and would all copies be changed simultaneously?" In case your answers vary depending on copies, you deal with coincidences rather than duplications.

This is not a novel concept. "Rule of three" was attributed to Don Roberts in Refactoring by Martin Fowler. The very first time you repeat some code, you just do it; the second time you wince but still do it; the third time, you refactor. Sandi Metz expressed the same beautifully in The Wrong Abstraction where she said that duplications are much cheaper than the wrong abstraction. Kent C. Dodds' AHA programming also suggests avoiding hasty abstractions.

Where reuse does pay off

This is not "never abstract". Some stuff is worth sharing from Day One:

  • Primitives that stay stable. Buttons, text inputs, layout containers. Small and boring interfaces; very little business logic contained within them.
  • Design tokens. Colors, spacing, and type scale exists to be used across multiple screens at once. That is the whole point of them.
  • Accessibility behavior. Focus trapping in dialogs, keyboard navigation, labelling. Getting it right once is better than getting it wrong slightly in five places.
  • Anything driven by a standard. Dates and times, currency formatting, protocol clients. Shape is defined externally, so the design of your next screen is less likely to distort it.

I distinguish such abstractions with these three criteria. Is the shape determined somewhere else than by my speculations on the future? Is there a single reason why it should be changed? Is it a component or a workflow?

The best smell test is always to read the list of props. If they describe what should be rendered (children, size, tone), then the abstraction is probably fine. If they are telling you in what situation you are (mode, variant, isSpecial), you have most likely combined several similar things into an abstraction.

How to recover from a premature abstraction

Start by inlining the common module back into each call site. Copy the module’s code to each workflow, and remove branches that workflow never takes. This approach is retrograde, but now all copies are short and easy to understand, and all workflows can be changed without permission from anybody else.

Next, separate the code according to the workflow rather than layout. Once the three codes are stabilized, find out what is now common due to the same reasons such as the table or date formatters and extract just the small pieces of code. This is also suggested by Metz in her essay.

The rule, once more

Copy and paste until the same pattern shows up three times for the same reason; but uncover the pattern first if you have got primitives, tokens, accessibility, and standardization.

So, the question that I want to ask you is: what is that piece of code which people dance around, and what is that special flag which you employ for that particular caller?
